question:
PySide6 Timing differences

(Updated to add an additional method of changing the label color and adding additional timing for original MWE. Added new version that uses a scene as suggested by @ekhumoro). I'm building a grid of labels that I can then continually change the background colors as values of the grid location changes. I have three different ways of getting the label in the specific grid location and then change its color. ChangeBox1 and ChangeBox2 use style sheets and ChangeBox3 directly changes the palette. When I call these routines while in the class init function, they run substantially faster than when I call them after displaying the window. Why? One can see that changeBox3 directly changing the palette is pretty consistent regardless of when it is called. Could this be a difference in how QT processes (or pyside translates) a style sheet after instantiating the widget? I'm using python 3.10.15 Average execution time of changeBox1 in init over 500 runs: 1.0947501286864281e-06 seconds Average execution time of changeBox2 in init over 500 runs: 4.599159583449364e-07 seconds Average execution time of changeBox3 in init over 500 runs: 2.514749765396118e-06 seconds Average execution time of changeBox1 after window.show over 500 runs: 1.4484249986708164e-05 seconds Average execution time of changeBox2 after window.show over 500 runs: 1.4263415709137917e-05 seconds Average execution time of changeBox3 after window.show over 500 runs: 2.624250017106533e-06 seconds Average execution time of myLabel1 over 500 runs: 1.668350026011467e-05 seconds Average execution time of myLabel2 over 500 runs:
reference_answer:
Biggest reason for why you're seeing this difference is due to the paintEvent() which is responsible for repainting a widget whenever an update is triggered. The first paint event, unless explicitly called prior to show() does not happen until after the call to show your window therefore any updates you make prior to display are not triggering any visual updates and repainting and will be handled during the first paint event. The paintEvent() is going to add time to the execution of visual updates as it will also trigger any children to be repainted as stylesheets themselves propagate. I'd recommend looking more into the paintevent Here is a screenshot with some example code and the time of paintEvent() and style updates prior to and after the first call to show(). import PySide6.QtWidgets as QtWidgets import shiboken6 class TestWin(QtWidgets.QMainWindow): def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) print("

Stylesheet set at initialization") win.setStyleSheet("") print("

Initialization Completed!") def paintEvent(self, *args, **kwargs): print("paintEvent() Called") super().paintEvent(*args, **kwargs) def setStyleSheet(self, *args, **kwargs): print("setStyleSheet() Called") super().setStyleSheet(*args, **kwargs)
llm_attempt: Style sheets (changeBox1/2 via setStyleSheet) go through Qt's CSS-like styling engine: each call re-parses the sheet and triggers a polish/unpolish plus style recomputation for the widget (and potentially cascades to children/ancestors depending on selectors). Before the window is shown, the widget isn't part of the live, laid-out render pipeline yet, so Qt can defer or short-circuit much of that work; once shown, the widget is actively painted, so setStyleSheet triggers real repaint scheduling and full re-evaluation each time, making it noticeably slower. changeBox3, which sets QPalette color roles directly, bypasses the style-sheet/CSS engine entirely - it's just a direct attribute write that Qt reads at paint time, so its cost doesn't depend on whether the widget is visible, explaining its consistency. This is a well-known QSS performance caveat: style sheets are convenient but expensive for frequent runtime updates, especially once shown. If you need fast, frequent color changes, prefer QPalette (or direct QPainter drawing) over setStyleSheet, and reserve style sheets for largely static styling set once at construction.

question:

I'm doing Angela Wu's course on Ubuntu. At day 16 she explains how to install a package into your project. (This one https://pypi.org/project/prettytable/ ) Then she proceeds to show how to do that in PyCharm (not sure what version she has there). She goes into PyCharm "settings" (I'm using Windows 10) and the clicks on her project in the main menu of those settings, after that she proceeds to look for Project Interpreter. (I somehow can't screenshot this). In any case, when I follow the steps, I cannot find my project in my settings. I've browsed the internet for a bit for solution and stumbled upon certain solutions like deleting the .idea folder which I tried, and when reopening PyCharm and .idea regeneration I still don't see my project in the settings.
reference_answer: you are likely using a modern PyCharm version with a slightly different UI, to configure the interpreter try Setting | Python | Interpreter ... ... or bottom-left interpreter widget ... given the interpreter is configured - you can install a package in View | Tool Windows | Python Packages
llm_attempt: This usually happens when PyCharm doesn't recognize your folder as an actual project - e.g. you opened a single file instead of using File > Open and selecting the project's root folder, so no .idea project was properly attached and Settings has no 'Project: <name>' node to expand. Recreating .idea won't help if the project itself was never opened correctly. Try File > Open, pick the top-level folder containing your code (not a file), let PyCharm index it, then reopen Settings/Preferences - you should see 'Project: <foldername>' with 'Python Interpreter' underneath (in recent PyCharm versions JetBrains renamed 'Project Interpreter' to 'Python Interpreter', so don't search for the old label). Also check whether you're looking at File > New Projects Settings by mistake - that configures defaults for future projects, not your current one. If multiple windows/projects are open, make sure Settings is opened from the window actually containing your project, not from the Welcome screen, which only shows global settings without a project node.

question:
AttributeError: Messagebox can't take multiple functions?

I tried to add multiple functions to a messagebox in my program: from Tkinter import * from Tkinter import messagebox as msgbox *some code...* input1 = msgbox.askyesno.showwarning('title', 'blahblahblah') if input1 == 1: input2 = msgbox.askyesno.showwarning('title', 'blahblahblah') if input2 == 1: function() But it shows me this error: input1 = msgbox.askyesno.showwarning('title', 'blahblahblah') ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ AttributeError: 'function' object has no attribute 'showwarning' I tried changing the order of the functions but it didn't help. Can anyone help??? EDIT: I got a comment saying it can't have multiple functions, so I guess i'll use VBS instead. Thanks for the help though! ANOTHER EDIT: I got it! I can just use this: title = "title" description = "blahblahblah" if MessageBox(description, title, MB_ICONWARNING | MB_YESNO) == IDNO: sys.exit(0)
reference_answer: I think, you're getting the error because askyesno is already a function inside tkinter.messagebox , not a module or object. So when you write msgbox.askyesno.showwarning(...) , you're trying to access .showwarning on a function, which doesn't make sense—hence the AttributeError . You need to call either askyesno or showwarning , depending on what you want the messagebox to do.
llm_attempt: askyesno and showwarning are two separate, independent functions in tkinter.messagebox - you can't chain them as msgbox.askyesno.showwarning(...). askyesno already returns True/False for a Yes/No dialog on its own: msgbox.askyesno('title', 'blahblahblah') pops the dialog and returns the user's choice directly. If you wanted a warning-style question box, use askyesno alone (it already reads like a warning question), or use showwarning alone if you just want an OK-only warning with no return value to branch on. So: input1 = msgbox.askyesno('title', 'blahblahblah'); if input1: ... Also, 'from Tkinter import *' with a capital T is Python 2 syntax; in Python 3 the module is lowercase 'tkinter', so if you're really on Python 3 that import should fail outright - double-check you're not mixing Python 2 and 3 examples. And prefer 'if input1:' over 'if input1 == 1:' since askyesno returns a bool, not necessarily the literal int 1.

question:
How to overload class member type depending on argument?

I recently learned I can overload return type using Literal[True] and Literal[False] argument. I am implementing my own subprocess.Popen -ish interface and I am not able to overload self.stdin return type to be IO[bytes] or IO[str] depending on the value of text in the constructor. I am using pyright for static type checking. I have tried the following: from typing import IO, Literal, Optional, overload class MyPopen: @overload def __init__(self, text: Literal[False] = False): self.stdin: Optional[IO[bytes]] @overload def __init__(self, text: Literal[True] = True): self.stdin: Optional[IO[str]] def __init__(self, text: bool = False): self.stdin = None pp = MyPopen(text=True) assert pp.stdin pp.stdin.write("text") # should be ok pp.stdin.write(b"text") # should error pp = MyPopen(text=False) assert pp.stdin pp.stdin.write("text") # should error pp.stdin.write(b"text") # should be ok However, it assumes pp.stdin to be IO[str] twice, and the declaration stdin is obscured: $ pyright /dev/stdin <1.py /dev/stdin /dev/stdin:7:14 - error: Declaration "stdin" is obscured by a declaration of the same name (reportRedeclaration) /dev/stdin:20:1 - error: No overloads for "write" match the provided arguments (reportCallIssue) /dev/stdin:20:16 - error: Argument of type "Literal[b"text"]" cannot be assigned to parameter "__s" of type "str" in function "write" "Literal[b"text"]" is incompatible with "str" (reportArgumentType) /dev/stdin:24:1 - error: No overloads for "write" match the provided arguments (reportCallIssue) /dev/stdin:24:16 - error: Argument of type "Literal[b"text"]" cannot b
reference_answer: I don't think this is valid use of @overload . It is used to specify more precise signatures for functions, not to conditionally set the type of attributes. However, you can create two empty subclasses, one for str and one for bytes , then let MyPopen.__new__() return either of those and use @overload on that instead. The subclasses don't have to do anything other than serving as types; the logic will still be defined in MyPopen . (playgrounds: mypy , Pyright ) # Or T = TypeVar('T', str, bytes); class MyPopen(Generic[T]): ... class MyPopen[T: (str, bytes)]: stdin: IO[T] | None # Now you can use @overload! @overload def __new__(cls, text: Literal[False] = ...) -> _BytesPopen: ... @overload def __new__(cls, text: Literal[True]) -> _StrPopen: ... def __new__(cls, text: bool = False) -> _BytesPopen | _StrPopen: if text is True: subclass = _StrPopen else: subclass = _BytesPopen # Use `object.__new__()` or `type: ignore` to pass strict mode instance = super().__new__(subclass) instance.stdin = None return instance def write(self, output: T) -> None: ... class _StrPopen(MyPopen[str]): pass class _BytesPopen(MyPopen[bytes]): pass The results will then be: pp = MyPopen() assert pp.stdin pp.stdin.write("text") # error: "Literal['text']" is incompatible with "bytes" pp.stdin.write(b"text") # fine pp = MyPopen(text=False) assert pp.stdin pp.stdin.write("text") # error: "Literal['text']" is incompatible with "bytes" pp.stdin.write(b"text") # fine pp = MyPopen(text=True) assert pp.stdin pp.stdin.write("text") # fine pp.stdin.write(b"text") # error: "Literal[b"text"]" is incompatible with
llm_attempt: Instance-attribute type narrowing based on which __init__ overload ran isn't supported this way - declaring self.stdin with different types inside separate @overload bodies doesn't work because attribute types are inferred from the single implementation's assignment, and pyright flags redeclaration. The typeshed-approved pattern (used by real subprocess.Popen) is to make the class generic: class MyPopen(Generic[AnyStr]) with self.stdin: Optional[IO[AnyStr]] declared once in __init__, then overload __new__ (not __init__) on the text: Literal[True]/Literal[False] parameter, returning MyPopen[str] and MyPopen[bytes] respectively (plus a fallback overload for text: bool). Callers then get MyPopen(text=True) inferred as MyPopen[str], so .stdin is IO[str], and MyPopen(text=False) as MyPopen[bytes], with .write() correctly rejecting the wrong type. This mirrors exactly how typeshed types subprocess.Popen's overloaded constructors and is the standard way to get argument-dependent generic return/attribute types checked correctly by pyright and mypy.

question:
Python, $PYTHONPATH, sys.path.add()

This code indicates what I wish to do, i.e., Have a variable to hold the name of a file to import, Use shutil.which() to look up the folder it resides in (via $PATH ), Automatically get that added to PYTHONPATH to make import find it. name = 'numbas' d = os.path.dirname(shutil.which(name + '.py')) sys.path.append(d) from name import * Now import does not allow a name stored in a variable. eval() on a string that contains the import statement is also "nonfunctional". How can I get this thing to actually work? The reason for all this is that I have *.py scripts in a Util/ folder, which are self-contained scripts and import modules for other scripts to utilize. If I move these around or copy them to a friend, I wish to have the folder structure remain as is.
reference_answer: Right, timez.py is used as a command line script, and by importing and calling main(): The fact that you get a "<module>" back from importlib.import_module(name) was not clear from the documentation I found. A type(...) revealed it though. I would have expected it to be added in the same manner as with a pure import . ./timez.py 10 1000 20 Output: ... has rotated 100.0 revs/hour at 2.0 rpm in average, while utilized 50.0% of the power hours. And: python -c "import importlib;name='timez'; timez=importlib.__import__(name);timez.main(['mama', 10, 1000, 20])" Output: ... has rotated 100.0 revs/hour at 2.0 rpm in average, while utilized 50.0% of the power hours. And: python -c "import importlib;name='timez'; timez=importlib.import_module(name);timez.main(['mama', 10, 1000, 20])" Output: ... has rotated 100.0 revs/hour at 2.0 rpm in average, while utilized 50.0% of the power hours.
llm_attempt: The import statement needs a literal identifier, not a variable, so 'from name import *' won't work. Use importlib instead: import importlib; mod = importlib.import_module(name). That returns the module object from a string name (after your sys.path.append(d) makes it discoverable), working with your shutil.which()-based path discovery exactly as intended. To use its contents, either reference mod.func_name directly, or emulate 'import *' by pulling names into your namespace: globals().update({k: v for k, v in vars(mod).items() if not k.startswith('_')}) (prefer using the module's __all__ list instead of the underscore filter if it defines one). Note this globals()-dump approach is fragile since it can silently shadow existing names, so prefer mod.attr access unless you specifically need bare names. You could also use importlib.util.spec_from_file_location to import directly from a known file path without touching sys.path/PYTHONPATH at all.

question:
Confusion about virtual environment and kernels in jupyter notebook

I created a virtual environment called "fastai" by conda. I tried to install ipywidgets in it by mamba install ipywidgets Then I checked it and it did exist. But when I used jupyter --version I found the status of ipywidgets was "Not installed". I guessed it might be the problem of jupyter kernel, and I registered a kernel for my virtual environment fastai: python -m ipykernel install --user --name fastai --display-name "Python (fastai)" I checked the new kernel by jupyter kernelspec list and it did succeed. Then I opened a notebook by jupyter notebook and shifted the kernel to the one I created with my virtual env fastai. But I stilled failed to import ipywidgets in the notebook. What's more, jupyter --version also kept that ipywidgets could not be found. I checked my widgetsnbextension, but found both the base env and the virtual env had already had it. That's what I got in my Powershell. I wonder what's going on, and how I can use ipywidgets in my virtual env successfully.
llm_attempt: 'jupyter --version' and its extension checks reflect whichever environment's 'jupyter' launcher/core you actually invoked in that shell - typically your base/default env, not 'fastai' - regardless of which kernel a notebook is later switched to. Registering a kernelspec makes the fastai Python selectable as a kernel, but the notebook server (jupyter core, notebook package, extensions) can still be running from base. Inside a notebook cell running under the 'Python (fastai)' kernel, run: import sys; print(sys.executable) - if that's not fastai's python.exe, you're not actually running fastai's code despite the kernel name. If it is fastai's interpreter but 'import ipywidgets' still fails, check that ipywidgets and jupyterlab_widgets/widgetsnbextension versions are compatible, and that the notebook server itself was launched from an environment that also has jupyterlab_widgets (or, for classic notebook, enable the extension with 'jupyter nbextension enable --py widgetsnbextension --sys-prefix' from within the fastai env).

question:
"TypeError: <class> is not reversible" -- what does it mean?

Something called reversed() on an instance of a class of mine, which resulted in the error TypeError: 'HBox' object is not reversible What does it mean for an object to be reversible?
reference_answer: Per the documentation for reversed() , a reversible object must either implement __reversed__ , or implement both __len__ and __getitem__ . The latter is preferable, unless it's less efficient.
llm_attempt: Python's reversed() only works on an object if it implements __reversed__(), or, failing that, if it implements both __len__() and __getitem__() (the sequence protocol), which lets Python synthesize a backward iterator by indexing from len-1 down to 0. If a class defines neither, reversed() has no way to traverse it backward and raises TypeError: '<ClassName>' object is not reversible. In your case, HBox (a container widget, e.g. from ipywidgets) apparently implements neither __reversed__ nor the full sequence protocol itself, so calling reversed() directly on the HBox instance fails even though it logically holds an ordered collection of children. The fix is to reverse the underlying sequence instead of the container: reversed(hbox.children) or hbox.children[::-1], since .children is typically a plain tuple that does support reversal. If HBox is your own class, add a __reversed__ method (e.g. return reversed(self._items)) or implement __len__/__getitem__ properly.

question:
what is the best way to produce a dynamic dictionary

I construct two files on Microsoft Excel. One containing Totonaco words with Spanish Meaning and the second one containing Spanish words with Totonaco meaning. I would like to know which is the optimal estructure to run just in my computer (not live in the web) as HTML page?
reference_answer: I have no idea what you want to do. You can create local web server using Flask , Django , Bottle , and many similar modules. If you run ML tasks then you may also use Streamlit , Dask , Gradio , etc. Everythink can run as local web server with HTML pages.
llm_attempt: For a bilingual Totonaco-Spanish dictionary that runs locally as a static HTML page (no server), the simplest robust structure is: use Python (pandas/openpyxl) to read both Excel files once and export them to a single JSON array, e.g. [{'totonaco': '...', 'spanish': '...'}], plus a reverse-lookup view generated the same way. Build one HTML file with a search input and a results div, and embed the JSON directly as a JavaScript variable inside a script tag in that HTML (rather than fetching a separate .json file) - this avoids browser CORS restrictions that block fetch()/XHR on file:// pages opened by double-click. Add a small JS function that filters the array on each keystroke (case-insensitive substring match on either language field) and re-renders matches. This gives an offline, dependency-free, double-click-to-run dictionary. If the wordlist grows very large and filtering feels slow, consider a prebuilt local search index (e.g. lunr.js bundled locally), but for a typical bilingual glossary plain JS array filtering is more than fast enough.

question:
Is there a way to plot a line that is a consistent length using matplotlib/cartopy?

I am using matplotlib and cartopy to draw lines overlaid on maps in python. As of right now, I am just identifying the lat/lon of two points and plotting a line between them. Since I am taking cross sections across these lines, I would like to find a way to make the line the same length (say 300km long) no matter where I place it on the map. Is this possible without just using trial and error and setting the points until they are the desired length? lat1, lat2, lon1, lon2 = [34.5, 36, -100, -97] x, y = [lon1, lon2], [lat1, lat2] ax1.plot(x, y, color="black", marker="o", zorder=3, transform = ccrs.PlateCarree(), linewidth = 2.5) Here are the relevant parts of the code that I am using now. This works, but I am looking for a way to hold the line length constant rather than changing the values for the endpoints at "lat1, lat2, lon1, lon2." I envision setting a line length, a mid-point (lat/lon), and an angle that would pivot around that point. I don't know if that's even possible, but that's how I'd imagine it'd have to work! Example of a line that the cross section would be through
reference_answer: The Geod class from pyproj is very convenient for these types of operations. The example below moves in a line from a given lat/lon based on an azimuth and distance (in meters). Since you mention starting with a mid-point, you can do this twice for each direction to get the full line. In the example below, I just retrieve the end points and use Cartopy ( ccrs.Geodetic() ) to do the interpolation to a great circle. But you can also do this yourself with the same Geod object ( see the npts method ), and sample a given amount of points a long the line. The latter might be convenient if you need those coordinates to extract data for example. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import cartopy.crs as ccrs from pyproj import Geod import numpy as np # start with a random point np.random.seed(0) lon = np.random.randint(-180,180) lat = np.random.randint(-90,90) # and a random direction and distance half_width = (1 + np.random.rand()) * 5000000 # meters azimuth = np.random.randint(0,360) # calculate the end points geod = Geod(ellps="WGS84") lon_end1, lat_end1, azi_rev1 = geod.fwd(lon, lat, azimuth, half_width) lon_end2, lat_end2, azi_rev2 = geod.fwd(lon, lat, azimuth-180, half_width) # visualize the result fig, ax = plt.subplots( figsize=(8,4), dpi=86, layout="compressed", facecolor="w", subplot_kw=dict(projection=ccrs.PlateCarree()), ) ax.set_title(f"{lon=}, {lat=}, {azimuth=}, {half_width=:1.1f}m") ax.plot( [lon_end1, lon, lon_end2], [lat_end1, lat, lat_end2], "ro-", transform=ccrs.Geodetic(), ) ax.coastlines() ax.set_global()
llm_attempt: Fixed lat/lon differences don't give a constant real-world distance because the length of a degree of longitude shrinks with latitude (and latitude spacing isn't perfectly uniform on an ellipsoid either), so you need geodesic math, not simple coordinate deltas. Use pyproj's Geod class: from pyproj import Geod; geod = Geod(ellps='WGS84'). Given a midpoint (lat0, lon0) and a bearing/azimuth in degrees, call geod.fwd(lon0, lat0, azimuth, distance_m) to get the endpoint exactly distance_m meters away along that bearing - call it twice, once with azimuth and once with azimuth+180, each using half your target length (150000 m for a 300 km line), to get two endpoints symmetric about the midpoint. Then plot those two points with ax1.plot([lon1,lon2],[lat1,lat2], transform=ccrs.Geodetic(), ...) - using ccrs.Geodetic() rather than PlateCarree ensures cartopy renders the true great-circle path. This lets you parametrize purely by center point, bearing, and length, with exact real-world distance regardless of map location.

question:
How to test langgraph Functional API entrypoints

In the official docs they only show how to test Graph API (StateGraph): https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/test#getting-started Our team is discussing alternatives to write such tests for the Functional API , especially regarding checkpointer injection. 1. Use builder to pass checkpointer To test entrypoints with InMemorySaver I decided to wrap each entrypoint function into a builder function like this: def wf1_builder(cp): @entrypoint(checkpointer=cp) async def wf1(...): ... return wf1 This way I can test them like this: async def test_wf1: wf1_test = wf1_builder(InMemorySaver()) result = await wf1_test.ainvoke(...) I think that this approach is analogous to the example tests that official docs show for Graph API. 2. Substitute checkpointer using copy If I define the entrypoint at 1st level, I could substitute the checkpointer e.g. with copy , although I don't like it because it looks like a hack. global_checkpointer = build_postgres_saver() @entrypoint(checkpointer=global_checkpointer) async def wf1(...): ... async def test_wf1: wf1_test = wf1.copy({ "checkpointer": InMemorySaver() }) result = await wf1_test.ainvoke(...) 3. question:
LSTM model prediction does not change with different inputs

I am implementing in PyTorch an LSTM model to predict if the closing value of a stock will go up or down in the next 5 and 10 minutes. Specifically, I am using 24 years of 5 minute data with 19 features, divided in chunks of one week per forecast (using 7 different stocks) The problem I'm facing is the fact that, no matter what, the LSTM model seems to predict values around one specific value to always minimize the loss, which it does not go down very much. I pre-prepare the inputs and targets in torch.tensors with [batch_size, sequence_len, features] (which in my case is [32, 2016, 19]), normalize them between 0 and 1 and feed them to my LSTM model which is structured like this: class MultiInputOutputLSTM(nn.Module): def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, output_size, dropout, lr, batch_size): super(MultiInputOutputLSTM, self).__init__() self.input_size = input_size self.hidden_size = hidden_size self.num_layers = num_layers self.dropout = dropout self.batch_size = batch_size self.loss_list = [] self.accuracy = 0 self.predictions_list = [0] self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size = self.input_size, hidden_size = self.hidden_size, num_layers = self.num_layers, dropout = self.dropout, batch_first=True) self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size, bias=True) self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid() self.criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() self.optimizer = torch.optim.RMSprop(self.parameters(), lr = lr, alpha=0.9, weight_decay=1e-4, momentum=0.5) self.scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(self.optimizer, 'min') def forward(self, x): h0 = torch.zeros(self.num_layers
llm_attempt: A very common cause of this exact symptom (predictions collapsing to one near-constant value) is applying Sigmoid twice: if forward() runs the output through self.sigmoid before returning it, and you then feed that into nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() (which already applies sigmoid internally to raw logits), you're squashing values twice - gradients through the doubly-saturated sigmoid vanish almost immediately, so the network stops learning and settles on whatever constant minimizes average loss. Fix: either return raw logits from forward() (no self.sigmoid call) and keep BCEWithLogitsLoss, or apply sigmoid in forward and switch to plain nn.BCELoss - never both. Separately, a sequence length of 2016 timesteps is extremely long for a vanilla LSTM; even with gating, gradients over that many steps tend to vanish or explode, independently pushing the model toward a trivial constant-output solution. Consider much shorter chunked sequences (or truncated BPTT), gradient clipping, and confirming your normalization doesn't collapse feature variance or the labels aren't heavily imbalanced.

question:
Using member functions of a class as LangGraph tools

I'm writing an agent using the LangChain and LangGraph libraries. I want to make my agent able to interact with files but only inside of the local directory, so I am writing a family of tools that are actually member functions of a class instance for storing the location of the local directory (which can be later expanded to have tracing/rollback functionality). The structure is as such: class FileInterface: def __init__(self): self.localdir = Path.cwd() # memorize local directory def get_tools(self): return [self.read_file,...] @tool def read_file(self, path:str) -> str: """tool for reading file at path""" if ... path is inside self.localdir ...: return path.read() etc. I then give the list to a langchain.agents.create_agent function to test the capabilities of this simple agent: file_interface = FileInterface() agent = create_agent( model=init_model(...), state_schema=MyState, tools=file_interface.get_tools(), system_prompt="You are a helpful agent [...]", checkpointer=InMemorySaver() ) print(agent.invoke({"messages":[{"role":"human","content":"tell me the contents of file example.txt"}]},context=context)) But when I invoke the agent with a query that prompts it to use one such tool I get the error: TypeError: StructuredTool._run() got multiple values for argument 'self' I would like to be able to have a family of tools that all refer to the data inside of an object. What is the intended way to achieve this? Here is the full traceback of an agent call with tool invocation: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/ubuntu/dev/elster/.venv/bin/elster", line 10, in <mod
reference_answer: You get that error because @tool on a bound instance method is not supported. When you decorate a method like: @tool def read_file(self, path: str) -> str: ... LangChain wraps it as a StructuredTool , but since it’s already bound (i.e. self is already attached), at runtime it gets passed another implicit self → so Python sees two self args → and thus: TypeError: StructuredTool._run() got multiple values for argument 'self' In a nutshell: tools need to be plain callables, not bound methods . So, To fix this you can wrap the instance method into a closure that captures self : class FileInterface: def __init__(self, base_dir: str): self.base_dir = Path(base_dir) def _read_file(self, filename: str) -> str: path = self.base_dir / filename return path.read_text() def tools(self): # ---- you must wrap in a closure like this ↓ ---- @tool def read_file(filename: str) -> str: """Read a file from disk inside base_dir""" return self._read_file(filename) return [read_file] here's a full working solution: from pathlib import Path from langchain_core.tools import tool from langchain.agents import create_agent from langchain_ollama.chat_models import ChatOllama class FileInterface: def __init__(self, base_dir: str): self.base_dir = Path(base_dir) def _read_file(self, filename: str) -> str: path = self.base_dir / filename return path.read_text() def tools(self): # ---- you must wrap in a closure like this ↓ ---- @tool def read_file(filename: str) -> str: """Read a file from disk inside base_dir""" return self._read_file(filename) return [read_file] # -------------- usage -------------- # 1)
llm_attempt: @tool captures the function's raw signature at decoration time, including 'self', turning it into a StructuredTool whose input schema then contains 'self' as a normal parameter. When the agent invokes the tool, LangChain supplies all schema-declared args as keyword arguments to the underlying callable - but since you're passing a bound method (self.read_file) as the implementation, Python's descriptor protocol already injects self as the first positional argument, so 'self' gets supplied twice: once implicitly by the bound method, once explicitly from the schema-derived kwargs, hence 'got multiple values for self'. Don't decorate instance methods directly. Instead, build closures inside get_tools() that capture instance state without exposing 'self' in the tool's signature: def get_tools(self): localdir = self.localdir; @tool def read_file(path: str) -> str: ...use localdir via closure...; return read_file; return [read_file, ...]. Now the tool's visible signature is just (path: str), with instance data captured via closure, avoiding the self-parameter conflict entirely.

question:
bash kernel dies in jupyter notebook

I am trying to use a bash kernel in jupyter notebooks and am receiving the following error: Connection failed A connection to the notebook server could not be established. The notebook will continue trying to reconnect. Check your network connection or notebook server configuration. I have tried the following workflow. From python command prompt: conda create --name bash_env --clone arcgispro-py3 conda install -c conda-forge bash_kernel python -m bash_kernel.install However, no matter what I try, I get a not connected error. I'm on Windows 11. jupyter kernelspec list returns: .net-csharp C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Roaming\jupyter\kernels\.net-csharp .net-fsharp C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Roaming\jupyter\kernels\.net-fsharp .net-powershell C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Roaming\jupyter\kernels\.net-powershell bash C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Roaming\jupyter\kernels\bash javascript C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Roaming\jupyter\kernels\javascript python3 C:\Users\myusername\AppData\Local\ESRI\conda\envs\bash_env\share\jupyter\kernels\python3 kernel.json within the above bash location reads: {"argv": ["C:\\Users\\myusername\\AppData\\Local\\ESRI\\conda\\envs\\bash_env\\python.exe", "-m", "bash_kernel", "-f", "{connection_file}"], "codemirror_mode": "shell", "display_name": "Bash", "env": {"PS1": "$"}, "language": "bash"} (Note: I have tried multiple alterations to kernel.json, including pointing to bash.exe, none of which have worked). I've also deleted that entire bash directory so that it reads it from the bash_env and it still didn't work. I have Git Bash downloaded and where b
llm_attempt: bash_kernel is built on pexpect, which spawns the shell through a POSIX pty - something native Windows doesn't provide outside WSL or Cygwin. On plain Windows, even inside a conda env with Git Bash installed, pexpect's spawn typically fails or the kernel process crashes immediately after start, which Jupyter surfaces as the generic 'Connection failed / reconnecting' message rather than a clear error, because the kernel died before establishing its heartbeat. This matches your symptoms: the kernelspec registers fine (that's just metadata) but the kernel process itself can't actually run. bash_kernel's own docs note it isn't supported on native Windows. The reliable fix is to run it under WSL: install WSL2 with a Linux distro, create your conda/venv and install bash_kernel there, register the kernelspec from inside WSL, and launch Jupyter from that WSL environment (or point the kernel's argv at WSL's bash). Pointing kernel.json at Git Bash's bash.exe generally doesn't work either, since pexpect still needs a real pty that Git Bash's MSYS layer doesn't fully expose to Windows-native Python.

llm_attempt: hello() calls the module-level logging.info(...), which writes wherever the root logger was configured via basicConfig() (filename='bandit.log') - not to your custom 'logger' object with the anomaly.log FileHandler, since that handler is only attached to the named logger you created inside logger(), not to the root logger. That's why nothing meaningful shows up in anomaly.log. The terkinter module is as follows: import tkinter as tk class Trk: """ The class of creating a canvas, and easily manipulating it with the TUI functions. """ global screenWidth, screenHeight def __init__(self,win,blocksx,blocksy,bg="#232627"): self.screenwidth = win.winfo_screenwidth() self.screenheight = win.winfo_screenheight() self.canvas = tk.Canvas(win,width=self.screenwidth,height=self.screenheight,background=bg) self.canvas.pack() self.background = bg self.parent = win self.winwidth = win.winfo_width() self.winheight = win.winfo_height() self.width = self.canvas.winfo_width() self.height = self.canvas.winfo_height() self.blockx = blocksx self.blocky = blocksy self.blocks = self.blockList() def coordinate(self,row,col): return row*self.blockx, (self.winheight-col)*self.blocky def blockList(self): li = [] for i in range(self.blockx): tmp = [] for j in range(self.blocky): tmp.append(None) li.append(tmp) return li def addText(self,row,col,text,font="1:1",color="white"): row, col = self
reference_answer: Why isn't the text showing? The terkinter module is as follows: It is because it is being drawn off-screen Your coordinates are calculated as 90, 5820. My monitor is only 2160 pixels tall. Unless your monitor is more than 5820 pixels tall you won't be able to see it. The culprit is the coordinates method combined with the values you've passed in. It's not clear what you're trying to do, but if you change coordinates to this, you'll see the text near the upper-left column: def coordinate(self,row,col): return row*self.blockx, col*self.blocky If you change it to this, it will appear at the bottom-left: def coordinate(self,row,col): return row*self.blockx, self.screenheight-(col*self.blocky)
llm_attempt: A very common cause of this pattern: Trk.__init__ computes self.winwidth, self.winheight, self.width, self.height by calling win.winfo_width()/winfo_height() and canvas.winfo_width()/winfo_height() immediately after creating the widgets - but at that point the window hasn't been drawn/mapped yet (you call win.geometry(...) and win.mainloop() afterward in your main script), so those winfo_* calls return bogus placeholder values (often 1). Since coordinate() computes pixel positions using self.winheight captured at that broken moment, addText() ends up placing text at wrong/degenerate coordinates - often off-canvas or collapsed near (0,0) - instead of where row/col=6,6 should map. The manual canvas.create_text(...) call using screenwidth/screenheight works because those come from win.winfo_screenwidth()/screenheight(), which don't depend on the window being mapped. Fix: call win.update_idletasks() right after win.geometry(...) and before constructing Trk(...), or better, compute width/height lazily rather than caching stale values from __init__.

llm_attempt: Your first pattern (calling session_maker() or session_maker.begin() fresh each time) is itself thread-safe and is the modern recommended SQLAlchemy style - each call creates an independent Session, so as long as you don't share one Session instance across threads/tasks, you're fine without scoped_session at all. scoped_session solves a different problem: it maintains a registry keyed by a 'scope' (by default threading.local(), i.e. current thread) and returns the same Session object for repeated calls within that scope, so code anywhere in that thread can call session_maker() and transparently get one shared, thread-local Session without passing it around explicitly - mainly useful for retrofitting older/global-style code (e.g. classic Flask-SQLAlchemy). You must call session_maker.remove() at the end of each unit of work to avoid leaking state into the next. async_scoped_session is the same idea for asyncio, but since there's no 'current thread' distinguishing concurrent coroutines, you must supply your own scopefunc (commonly asyncio.current_task). For new async code, explicit per-request sessionmaker() is usually simpler and preferred.
